title: the Brahmanda
hook: two tellings of Sita, and the argument people have about them
tomorrow: a fish, a tortoise, a boar: why is a row of animals one god?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Brahmanda, and a hymn made of names: Shri Mata first, then a portrait one name at a time. Today, one more book tradition places in this Purana, and an argument people have about it.

Every fandom has the fight over which version is the real one. Rama's story has one too. In the Adhyatma Ramayana, which tradition places in the Brahmanda Purana, Shiva tells Rama's story to Parvati, and it runs the familiar road: the exile, the forest, the golden deer. Then, just before Ravana comes, Rama asks Sita to go into the fire for safekeeping and leave a likeness of herself behind. The Sita that Ravana carries off to Lanka is the likeness. The real Sita waits, untouched, until the fire gives her back.
screen: `WHICH VERSION IS THE REAL ONE?` → `SITA GOES INTO THE FIRE.` → `RAVANA TAKES A LIKENESS.`

segments.voice: Adhyatma means having to do with the self, the inner side of things. This telling keeps pausing so someone can say who Rama really is: the supreme Self, come in a human life, with Sita as his power. The likeness fits that. In Valmiki's Ramayana, though, the Sita Ravana takes is Sita herself. So people who love this story weigh the two tellings, and both sides have a real case. Here's the first, at its best. Sita is the goddess. Nothing Ravana does can touch her, and the likeness says so in story form. It spares her, it spares the devotee who can't bear to picture her a prisoner, and it fits a book whose whole point is the truth under the events. Now the second, at its best. In Valmiki, the real Sita is taken, and she stays herself: she refuses Ravana, she waits, she holds on in a garden full of guards. Her courage is the point. A likeness, this side says, takes away the very thing that makes her a hero. The tradition keeps both. Some read the Adhyatma aloud, some read Valmiki, and some read both and live with the tension. And notice what the two sides agree on: Sita is never Ravana's. They only disagree about how the story shows it.
screen: `ADHYATMA: THE INNER SIDE.` · `CASE ONE: NOTHING CAN TOUCH HER.` · `CASE TWO: HER COURAGE IS THE POINT.` · then, large: `BOTH AGREE: SITA IS NEVER RAVANA'S.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Think of something you and someone close to you see differently, and write their side in one sentence, as well as they'd put it themselves. Read it back once, slowly, and let it stand. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
The Brahmanda: the Purana of Brahma's egg, where tradition places a Ramayana told from the inside.
The line to take with you: the Brahmanda, the same story with its inner side showing. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Adhyatma Ramayana is read and recited by some Rama devotees, especially for its hymns and its teaching passages; Valmiki's Ramayana and many other tellings are read alongside it.

fork.setup: your friend loves the Adhyatma's likeness. state the other side's best case in one line.
options: in Valmiki, the real Sita is taken and stays herself; her courage is the point.

fork.reveal: that's the Valmiki side at its best: a Sita who is really there, refusing Ravana and holding on. both sides agree she is never his.

original.note: Sanskrit adhyatma: having to do with the self, the inner side. It names this Ramayana.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one Ramayana, and it's Valmiki's.
what it means: there are many tellings; the Adhyatma walks the same road with its inner side showing.
what a scholar hears: the Adhyatma Ramayana, framed as Shiva to Parvati and placed by tradition in the Brahmanda Purana, with the likeness of Sita at its turn.
